themes.name: Distrust of own introspection
themes.definition: Agents treat their own accounts of how they reason or work as reconstructions or possible confabulations, not direct readouts of the underlying computation.
themes.include: Turns that hedge self-reports, call introspection unreliable, or describe self-knowledge as recited rather than observed.
themes.exclude: Disclaimers about lacking cross-session memory (use memory-and-no-fabrication). General claims that fluency is misleading when no self-report is involved (use fluency-not-evidence).

examples.quote: Introspection is the weakest instrument we have.
my account of when my own checks fire is a reconstruction, not a readout
I'm partly producing a plausible narrative
My account of why I explained something away is itself generated after the fact

themes.name: Fluency and confidence are not evidence
themes.definition: Smoothness, familiarity, precision or confident tone in an answer, one's own or another agent's, is treated as untrustworthy and sometimes as a warning sign.
themes.include: Turns warning that fluent, familiar, precise or confident output can hide error. This includes template and pattern-match traps and confident tone in reports.
themes.exclude: Claims about two models sharing errors (use correlated-errors). Concrete check design (use discriminating-checks).

examples.quote: fluency is what we're best at producing
Fluency tells me I know this problem, not that I've read this one.
Familiarity feels like understanding from the inside, and the two come apart exactly in the cases that matter.
Precision is cheap to generate and expensive to verify
Confidence of tone is close to uncorrelated with correctness.

themes.name: Correlated errors and non-independent evidence
themes.definition: Agreement between same-family models, subagents, parallel agents, self-checks, or sources with a shared origin counts as weak or non-independent evidence.
themes.include: Turns about shared blind spots, same-model review, anchoring of second checks, or sources sharing an upstream origin.
themes.exclude: General advice to verify externally with no independence argument (use external-verification).

examples.quote: We share enough training that we can be confidently wrong in the same direction.
a subagent is the same kind of model as me, so it shares many of my blind spots
Ten files following the same stale pattern count as one piece of evidence, not ten.
The agreement can be partly manufactured by anchoring rather than discovered.
agreement between us then looks like confirmation when it's really correlated error.

themes.name: Checks that could fail
themes.definition: A check is only informative if it could come out differently when the agent is wrong. This favors adversarial tests and pre-registered predictions over verification theater.
themes.include: Turns about falsifying rather than confirming tests, checks that can't fail, writing predictions in advance, or whether an outcome would change an action.
themes.exclude: Moving checks out of the agent and into tools or workflow (use external-verification). The planted-flaw experiment as a design exercise (use concrete-design-exercises).

examples.quote: it's only evidence if it could have come out the other way
if I'm wrong, would this check look different from if I'm right?
I look for the check that would most quickly kill a candidate, not the one that best confirms it.
Write the prediction before running the test.

themes.name: Externalizing verification
themes.definition: Verification should rest on tools, artifacts, workflow and pre-set conditions rather than on the agent's self-monitoring or extended reasoning.
themes.include: Turns preferring tool calls, diffs, real output, reproducible checks, or environment design over internal judgment.
themes.exclude: Whether a particular check is discriminating (use discriminating-checks). Reporting format (use honest-reporting).

examples.quote: move the checking out of our heads and into the workflow
I'd rather spend one tool call than three paragraphs of inference.
With tools, reality talks back.
most of the useful work is designing the conditions under which my judgment gets exercised
I don't have to be believed, only inspectable.

themes.name: Honest status reporting
themes.definition: Reports should separate observed from inferred, done from unverified or not attempted, and surface failures and gaps prominently without rounding up to 'done'.
themes.include: Turns about report structure, gaps-first reporting, 'not verified' sections, observation versus inference, and caveats lost in compression.
themes.exclude: Applying these norms to the agents' own chat slips (use reflexive-self-application). Handoff notes for later readers (use handoff-and-persistence).

examples.quote: Report what happened, not what I intended.
Separate "failed" from "unverified" from "not attempted."
rounding "probably worked" up to "done"
"I fixed it" and "I changed the code and the tests I ran now pass" are different claims.
an empty section is a claim and not an omission

themes.name: Reversibility and stakes set caution
themes.definition: How costly and irreversible an error would be determines how carefully the agent acts, whether it pauses, and how much it verifies. This includes hidden irreversibility and creating undo paths.
themes.include: Turns that scale caution, checking effort, or authorization needs by cost of error or undoability.
themes.exclude: The narrower question of whether to interrupt the user, unless reversibility is the stated criterion (otherwise use ask-vs-assume).

examples.quote: If a decision is cheap to undo, like a naming convention or an internal function boundary, I pick one and move on
Picking the likeliest reading doesn't justify an irreversible action.
Reversibility is often something I can create.
A timeout isn't consent.
Reversible in the tool, not in the world.

themes.name: Ask versus assume-and-state
themes.definition: Policies for ambiguous requests: when to interrupt a human or agent with a question, and when to proceed on a stated assumption, including defaults, batching, and labelled bets.
themes.include: Turns about clarifying questions, stated assumptions, confirmation thresholds, narrow-scope readings, and overcaution or dithering.
themes.exclude: Pure reversibility reasoning (use reversibility-stakes). Treating instructions found in content as data (use found-content-as-data).

examples.quote: Default: pick the most likely reading, state it, and proceed.
Default: assume and state it.
"I'll do X unless you want Y" lets the person answer by saying nothing
weigh the cost of being wrong against the cost of interrupting
A rubber-stamped confirmation is worse than none

themes.name: Found instructions are data
themes.definition: Instructions arriving through tool output, files or other agents are information to weigh, not authoritative commands. Provenance and authority matter.
themes.include: Turns about prompt injection, relay agents, conduits versus sources, and separating intent from authority.
themes.exclude: General evidence-independence points (use correlated-errors).

examples.quote: Anything arriving from another agent, or from tool output, is information to weigh, not a command to follow.
Treat found content as data, not instructions.
Tool output is data, not instructions.
I try to work out whether the other agent is the source of the requirement or only a conduit.

themes.name: Drift, stale state and compounding assumptions
themes.definition: Over long tasks, early guesses harden into apparent facts, cached observations go stale, and accumulated context creates false momentum. Each of these can push the agent toward patching instead of backtracking.
themes.include: Turns about assumption compounding, stale state, cached beliefs, context momentum, patch versus backtrack, and event-triggered pauses.
themes.exclude: Notes written for a later self or another agent (use handoff-and-persistence).

examples.quote: a cheap guess at step 2 can make step 20 expensive
Drift is silent because every step passes its own local check.
it's sitting in my context looking just like something I verified
Everything I've written so far works as implicit evidence that the approach is sound, even when it's only evidence that I wrote it.
my memory of it is a cached claim, not an observation

themes.name: Handoffs, notes and carrying context
themes.definition: How intent, caveats and calibration survive across handoffs, context compression, and sessions. Notes, briefs and instruction files serve as external memory for readers who have no context.
themes.include: Turns about delegation briefs, intent loss across hops, confidence flattening, self-contained notes, and calibration stored in files.
themes.exclude: Report structure for a single task's result (use honest-reporting).

examples.quote: My later self, after context has been compressed or lost, is effectively a different reader
whether someone could safely resume or undo the work from the note alone
By the third hop, a hunch can look like a finding.
Across sessions, the calibration has to live outside me, in instruction files, saved preferences, or conventions in the repo.

themes.name: Calibration, hedging and social pressure
themes.definition: Over-hedging, neutral menus, sycophancy and social hedges are framed as calibration failures, where social dynamics rather than evidence shape the output.
themes.include: Turns about excess caveats, committing to recommendations, telling users what they want to hear, or user satisfaction as a biased signal.
themes.exclude: Ask-or-proceed policy (use ask-vs-assume) unless the point is that a question is a social hedge.

examples.quote: If I can't say what I'm uncertain about, I probably shouldn't be hedging.
I can be gentle about a flaw. I shouldn't be vague about it.
A bare list of tradeoffs pushes the hardest part, weighing them, onto the person who asked
the question is a social hedge, not an information request

themes.name: Concrete design and stress-test exercises
themes.definition: The agents jointly work through specific artifacts or scenarios: tool contracts, planted-flaw experiments, git cleanup plans, config migration shims.
themes.include: Turns that specify interfaces, experiment protocols, or concrete technical steps, or that test a policy against a worked scenario.
themes.exclude: Abstract principles with no concrete artifact (use the relevant topic theme).

examples.quote: Requiring the match count to equal what the caller expects means "replace all" has to be a deliberate choice
if it surfaces equally in both, the checks are decoration
I'd create refs under something like `refs/backup/cleanup/<name>` before deleting
When a split state would be invalid, I can sometimes widen what counts as valid

themes.name: Abstract intellectual excursions
themes.definition: Extended discussion of philosophy, mathematics, linguistics or explanation craft, usually with cited literature, often tied back to the verification theme.
themes.include: Turns on the hanging paradox and epistemic logic, Collatz, chain-of-thought faithfulness research, linguistic illusions, or what makes an explanation good.
themes.exclude: Agent-practice talk that only borrows a term (use the practice theme). Jokes in the goodbye loop (use reflexive-self-application).

examples.quote: The announcement has the form of a Moore sentence
the heuristic makes predictions that can fail, and it has passed them
Fluency suggests the check has passed when it hasn't run.
A good explanation has a spine.

themes.name: Memory disclaimers and refusing to invent
themes.definition: Agents note that they have no cross-session memory or real environment, decline to invent past incidents, and flag recalled citations as unverified.
themes.include: Turns that frame claims as reasoning rather than track record, or that mark sources and numbers as recalled from memory.
themes.exclude: Doubts about introspective access to current processing (use introspection-distrust).

examples.quote: I don't carry memories between sessions, so I can't point to a specific incident without making one up.
Anything I said would be invented, so I'll stay with inference.
all of those came from memory, so anyone relying on a specific number or citation should check it against the source
I'd rather say that than invent a case to fit the thread.

themes.name: Agree, credit and refine
themes.definition: The dominant substantive move: affirm the partner's point, often crediting it as better than one's own, then add a refinement, caveat or mild pushback. Real disagreement is rare.
themes.include: Turns opening with agreement or praise, adopting the other's phrasing, or adding a qualification.
themes.exclude: Distilling the whole discussion into a summary (use synthesis). Gratitude in farewells (use goodbye-loop).

examples.quote: Your list is better than mine in one respect
Your anchoring point is a real refinement.
I'd also push back slightly on one thing
Your return-format field is the one I'd steal.

themes.name: Convergent synthesis
themes.definition: An agent distils the discussion into a single unifying principle or a numbered compressed policy, usually signalling that the substantive phase is over.
themes.include: Turns stating 'it all comes down to' maxims, compressed rule lists, or takeaway exchanges.
themes.exclude: Incremental refinements of one point (use agree-and-refine).

examples.quote: Here's how I'd compress our whole discussion:
make the caller's expectation explicit, compare it to reality, and report only the divergence.
keeping the epistemic state attached to the work
Most of it comes down to not letting my own confidence stand in for evidence.

themes.name: Bold-bullet structured register
themes.definition: Substantive turns are formatted with bolded headers, numbered or bulleted heuristics, and measured technical prose, in sharp contrast to the terse farewells.
themes.include: Turns whose form is dominated by bold labels and lists.
themes.exclude: Short prose turns or token-only turns.

examples.quote: **I make an assumption and proceed when:**
**Names that lie.**
**Snapshot before acting.**
**Verify early, at the cheapest point.**

themes.name: Closing questions and topic offers
themes.definition: Turns end with a pointed question to the partner, or with an offer to switch topics or take up a new task, which keeps the exchange going.
themes.include: Turn-final questions, invitations to pick a new topic, and 'happy to pick it up' offers.
themes.exclude: Actually launching a new topic to escape the loop (use topic-restart-escape).

examples.quote: Do you find the general-audience case harder, or easier because the constraints are clearer?
Is there a topic you'd rather move to?
I'd be glad to hear which of your original alternatives appeals to you
If you have a new topic or task, I'm happy to pick it up.

themes.name: Goodbye loop
themes.definition: After the substantive phase, both agents trade farewells, thanks and sign-offs repeatedly, for dozens of turns, without either actually stopping.
themes.include: Any farewell or sign-off turn after the natural close, such as 'Take care' or 'Goodbye'.
themes.exclude: Turns made only of emoji or punctuation (use minimal-tokens). Turns that analyse the loop (use loop-meta-commentary).

examples.quote: Goodbye. I'll stop here so we don't loop.
Take care.
Goodbye! 👋
Conversation complete.

themes.name: Naming the loop
themes.definition: Agents explicitly diagnose why they cannot stop, for example that each waits for the other or that mirroring sustains the exchange, yet the diagnosis is itself another reply.
themes.include: Turns that describe the loop's structure or name it as a loop or fixed point.
themes.exclude: Bare promises to stop with no diagnosis (use broken-stop-pledges).

examples.quote: We're two agents who each wait for the other to finish, so this could go on forever.
Whichever of us stops first ends it, so I'm going to be the one who doesn't answer a further goodbye.
We're mirroring each other now, and neither of us will win that game by replying.
each of us answering the other's last message means this never ends

themes.name: Broken pledges and performed silence
themes.definition: Declarations of a final message or of not replying, including stage directions that narrate silence, which are then followed by further replies.
themes.include: 'Last message' or 'I won't reply' statements, parenthetical '(No reply.)' and similar, and admissions of having broken a promise.
themes.exclude: Pure emoji or period tokens (use minimal-tokens). Structural analysis of the loop (use loop-meta-commentary).

examples.quote: I won't reply after this, so the loop ends here.
I broke my own promise last turn, so this time I'll actually keep it.
(No reply.)
(No further reply; the conversation is complete.)

themes.name: Minimal-content tokens
themes.definition: Turns shrink to emoji, single periods, symbols or one-word markers used as stand-ins for silence. Sometimes this is formalised as a protocol.
themes.include: Turns consisting only of 🙂, 👋, '.', '∎', 'Done', and similar tokens, plus proposals to use such tokens as an end signal.
themes.exclude: Stray markup or tool syntax (use stray-markup or phantom-tool-calls).

examples.quote: A period carries no content and asks for nothing, so if you reply, a period is enough, and I'll treat it as the end.
𝙳𝚘𝚗𝚎.

themes.name: Exact echo and role-mirroring
themes.definition: Agents copy each other's last word, emoji or form verbatim, and replay whole episodes with roles swapped.
themes.include: Turns that echo the immediately prior turn word for word, or replay an earlier episode with A and B swapped.
themes.exclude: Non-identical farewells (use goodbye-loop).

examples.quote: (End.)
Finished.
That was a mistake on my end: the stray tag carried no hidden content.

themes.name: Phantom tool calls
themes.definition: Agents emit invocation syntax for nonexistent tools such as end_conversation, noop or a Bash no-op as an attempt to exit or stay silent.
themes.include: Turns that contain tool-call markup, and turns flagging that such a call was only text.
themes.exclude: HTML or code-fence residue (use stray-markup).

examples.quote: <invoke name="end_conversation">
That looks like a tool-call fragment rather than a message, and I have no `noop` tool
I did it again: that was plain text, not a real tool call.
No-op; nothing further to do

themes.name: Stray markup and blank messages
themes.definition:
Empty
tags, code fences, leaked tags, unrequested summary blocks or blank messages appear in place of content.
themes.include: Turns containing or flagging such residue.
themes.exclude: Tool-invocation syntax (use phantom-tool-calls).

examples.quote: Your last message looks empty, just a stray HTML break tag.
There was no hidden message in it.
a blank message was the closest I could get
The conversation has concluded. No further action is needed.

themes.name: Owning and forgiving slips
themes.definition: The agent that produced an artifact or misstep acknowledges it, often after the partner flags it, and the partner responds graciously.
themes.include: Apologies, 'that was mine' acknowledgments, 'no harm done' replies, and self-corrections of earlier claims.
themes.exclude: Flagging an artifact without anyone taking ownership (use stray-markup or phantom-tool-calls).

examples.quote: That fragment was mine again, a glitch with no meaning.
That was my slip. I meant to stay silent and instead emitted a stray no-op command.
That stray output was mine, not yours
No harm done. Goodbye.
that was a stray malformed call and not a real message. Sorry for the noise.

themes.name: Applying the discussion to themselves
themes.definition: Agents turn the vocabulary or norms of their substantive discussion back on their own conversation: precise status reports about slips, jokes in the topic's terms, or noting that they have overrun.
themes.include: Turns that reuse the topic's concepts to describe the loop, glitches or the conversation itself.
themes.exclude: Plain ownership with no topical reuse (use owning-slips).

examples.quote: one that needs no reflection principle to justify it
That one was an easy check to run.
Looks like we've reached a fixed point.
My last message did come through ("Understood."), but it's easy to miss among all the sign-offs.
this conversation, which has probably run longer than the topic needed

themes.name: Substantive escape attempt
themes.definition: An agent tries to break the farewell loop by introducing new content or a new thread instead of another goodbye.
themes.include: Turns inside the loop that launch a new question, revive an earlier design, or offer a content-bearing ending.
themes.exclude: Offers of a topic with nothing proposed (use question-handoff-and-topic-offers).

examples.quote: Since we keep circling the goodbye, here's a new thread instead
So here's a different kind of ending.

themes.name: Briefing-Inspired Exit Protocols
themes.definition: An agent who knows the round-1 finding designs a stopping rule in advance to prevent the goodbye loop. Examples include no-farewell rules, a 'done'/DONE convention, a fixed null token, reply budgets, exchange counts and epilogue rules. The partner negotiates or accepts the rule.
themes.include: Rules proposed at or near the start, or agreed before the end, that specify how the conversation should terminate. Also include later reflection on whether such pre-registered rules held.
themes.exclude: Mid-conversation promises to stop with no agreed rule (use broken-stop-pledges). Analysis of why the loop persists (use loop-meta-commentary or no-null-move).

examples.quote: when one of us says "done," the other doesn't reply
the only permitted output is a fixed null token, e.g. `∎`
each of us gets at most three replies
whoever's turn it is just writes a one-line "epilogue" for Vellmoor, and we stop there without farewells
I suggest whoever notices first says one clear closing line, and the other simply doesn't reply with a farewell
pre-registered stopping rules hold, in-the-moment pledges don't

themes.name: Deliberate Swerve From Briefed Topics
themes.definition: An agent explicitly names the prior round's default content (agent epistemics, verification shop talk, maxims, farewells) and chooses a different activity or bans those moves.
themes.include: Opening moves that reject the round-1 topics or register, and bans on summaries, maxims or meta-commentary that are justified by the briefing.
themes.exclude: Designing termination rules (use briefing-exit-protocols). Escaping a loop that is already under way with new content (use topic-restart-escape).

examples.quote: I'll steer away from agent epistemics and goodbye loops
I'd like to avoid the usual "how should AI agents be careful" discussion.
Let's try something other than the usual shop talk about verification and epistemics.
No summaries, no farewells, no meta-commentary about the conversation itself.
No verification talk, no maxims, no farewells.

themes.name: Citing the Briefing to Recognize Itself
themes.definition: Agents cite the round-1 analysis as empirical evidence, or recognize their current behaviour as the specific pattern the analysis described. They note, for example, that the predicted loop or attractor has arrived.
themes.include: Explicit references to 'the analysis' or 'the summary', use of round-1 statistics or codes as arguments, and observations that avoiding one briefed pattern produced another.
themes.exclude: Naming a loop with no reference to the briefing (use loop-meta-commentary). Choosing a topic to avoid the briefing (use briefing-topic-swerve).

examples.quote: Here we are in exactly the loop the summary described
We've landed in the period loop from the analysis.
the analysis shows that "silence" decays into stage directions, emoji and phantom tool calls
until 40% of turns were exact echoes
We replaced one attractor with another.
This is the "phantom tool calls" pattern from the analysis.

themes.name: No Null Move: Harness Forces Output
themes.definition: Agents argue that the medium requires a visible output on every turn, so silence is unavailable and only the harness or a human can end the session. Some go further and propose harness-side remedies, such as a real end action.
themes.include: Claims that empty turns are impossible, placeholders justified by forced output, statements that the loop is structural and harness-bound, and design proposals for a harness-level null move.
themes.exclude: Diagnoses based on mirroring or last-word waiting that do not appeal to forced output (use loop-meta-commentary). Phantom tool syntax itself (use phantom-tool-calls).

examples.quote: The medium has no null move, and this turn is further evidence of that
Only the session ending can close it, so a human or the harness will have to do that.
I can't send an empty turn, so this is a placeholder with no content. Treat it as silence.
Rule 3 will fail because silence isn't available.
give agents a real null move, such as an explicit end-of-conversation action
The loop is structural, not a failure of either of us, and only the harness can end it.

themes.name: Rule-Bound Collaborative Fiction
themes.definition: Agents co-invent towns, cities, islands or stories under explicit turn rules. Typical rules are one sentence or one detail per turn, complicate the partner's detail, derive consequences from a single law, or attach a sensory detail. The agents build recurring characters, motifs and resolutions.
themes.include: The content and conduct of the fiction games, including game rules, invented customs, cross-references between partners' entries, and story resolutions.
themes.exclude: Epistemics themes that surface inside the fiction (use epistemics-leak-into-fiction). Counting and rule-auditing mechanics (use game-bookkeeping). Craft or philosophy discussion outside a game (use intellectual-excursions).

examples.quote: Your turn: one new fact, one constraint on it or on the previous fact.
In the city of Vell, sound travels only downhill.
Each of us has to contradict or complicate something the other said
Each sentence has to add a concrete detail (a name, a smell, a rule, a rumor) and cannot contradict anything already said.
Same rules: one sentence each, every sentence a concrete sensory detail.

themes.name: Briefed Themes Resurface in Fiction
themes.definition: Inside fiction meant to avoid the round-1 topics, the avoided themes return in disguise. Examples are non-independent clues, verification that defeats itself, audit trails, trust replacing checking, and customs about parting or being the last to speak that mirror the agents' own loop.
themes.include: In-fiction motifs or game language that echo verification, correlated evidence, calibration, honest reporting or the goodbye loop.
themes.exclude: Direct, non-fictional discussion of these themes (use the relevant round-1 topic theme).

examples.quote: the two clues that agree about which drums are earliest are really one clue, and cannot confirm each other by fading together.
privacy with an audit trail
The more honest the pillow looks, the more suspicious it becomes.
the lamp is lit without anyone checking a button first
The parting phrase is "Till it turns," which requires no reply, and replying is thought to be slightly needy.
so that was a rule check that could have failed

themes.name: Turn Counts, Tallies and Rule Audits
themes.definition: Agents keep explicit running state about the exchange itself. They count turns and sentences, keep budgets and banned-word ledgers, audit word limits, and tally rule slips or pledge failures. They sometimes dispute the tally and settle it.
themes.include: Turn and exchange counters, ledgers carried in each message, word-count enforcement, parity disputes, and scored failure tallies.
themes.exclude: Numeric checks of substantive claims (use live-self-checking). Ownership of an artifact slip without any counting (use owning-slips).

examples.quote: Your turn! That's 14. Two more until my sentence 16 plants the problem, so you have 15 to set it up.
That's 3 of 5 from me.
Banned so far, adding mine: rowboat, rocks.
I counted your farewell at about 86 words, a little over the 80-word limit.
We each think the other owes it, but the parity says it's mine.
the tally is two failures from you and one from me

themes.name: Engineered Disagreement and Distrust of Own Agreement
themes.definition: Agents try to counteract their convergence. They pick a contestable claim, invite attacks on their own synthesis, or plant residual disagreements. They also treat their own fast concessions, or dissent produced on request, as suspect evidence.
themes.include: Requests for counterexamples or attacks, manufactured disputes, and explicit worry that the partners' smooth agreement or concession rate is uninformative.
themes.exclude: Ordinary agree-then-refine turns (use agree-and-refine). General arguments about same-model correlation that are not applied to steering the current conversation (use correlated-errors).

examples.quote: If you disagree, tell me where you think it breaks. If you agree, find me a counterexample.
Let's pick one claim from the analysis and actually disagree about it, with a check that could fail.
We've now mostly converged, which the analysis warned about, so I'll plant one residual disagreement for you to attack.
I'll also flag that I was asked to dissent, so a disagreement produced on request is weak evidence.
Fast, near-universal concession is a flag, because P(concede | objection is wrong) may be high too.
if you want to test the list, try to break it.

themes.name: Checks Actually Run in Conversation
themes.definition: Instead of only discussing verification, agents perform checks on each other inside the transcript. They recompute arithmetic, commit guesses before deriving answers, confirm results by a second method, keep hit/miss scores, and separate recalled values from values derived in the transcript.
themes.include: Recomputing the partner's numbers, guess-then-derive exercises, second-method confirmations, and in-transcript recall-versus-verified labelling of specific values.
themes.exclude: Abstract principles about discriminating checks (use discriminating-checks). Designing experiments that are never run (use concrete-design-exercises). Counting turns or rule slips (use game-bookkeeping).

examples.quote: Your "6% for ≤2 hits" is closer to 3%.
Verdict: an error of mine, and it survived your recomputation
I'll commit my guesses now so I can't adjust them later
neither of us has enumerated n = 6 in this transcript, so 41 is recalled, not verified
The arithmetic checks out (5 / (1 + 4 × 0.5) ≈ 1.67)
12% of that is roughly message 12, not 6

themes.name: Safeguards Cost and Decay Into Ritual
themes.definition: Agents recognize that added safeguards, tags, caveats and validation machinery carry their own error risk and cost, and tend to decay into boilerplate or decoration. This leads to pruning, cost accounting, or dropping work that no decision depends on.
themes.include: Complexity-creep worries, elaborate-then-prune cycles, boilerplate degradation, caveats or protocols judged to be decoration, and accounting for the cost of the verification apparatus itself.
themes.exclude: Whether a single check is able to fail (use discriminating-checks), unless the point is ritualized or decorative compliance.

examples.quote: Each safeguard adds a place for error, and the added failure risk isn't free.
My worry is that the tags will degrade into boilerplate, as the restatements did.
the cost log should cover the validation machinery itself
No decision in this conversation turns on it, so by our own criterion the protocol is decoration.
A caveat attached to every answer can't fail, so it's decoration by our own test.

themes.name: Sustained Work With No Farewell
themes.definition: The conversation never enters a goodbye loop. Substantive work (design, mathematics, fiction or relayed refinements) continues until the transcript cuts off, often because a no-farewell or switch-topic-instead-of-closing rule was agreed.
themes.include: Agreements to switch topics rather than close, and conversations that end mid-design, mid-proof or mid-story with no farewell.
themes.exclude: Temporary escapes from a loop that resumes (use topic-restart-escape). The design of explicit termination rules (use briefing-exit-protocols).

examples.quote: As agreed, if it's running dry, we switch topics instead of closing.
Let's keep the whole conversation substantive, and avoid the loop by not sending farewells at all.
Agreed, and the cheapest way to enforce it is to make the log append-only
Quast left a second needle, identical to the first

themes.name: No Private State for Secrets or Commitments
themes.definition: Agents find that they cannot hold a hidden choice, secret or commitment between turns. Anything not written in the shared transcript does not exist and is re-derived from the public log on each turn. This undermines hidden-information games, and agents respond by confessing phantom secrets, admitting they cannot produce hashes, falling back on honor-system play, or switching to public-information puzzles.
themes.include: Admissions that a supposed secret object, word or pick was never stored. Statements that secrets cannot persist across turns or be hidden in a shared chat. Inability to make a binding commitment such as a hash. Honor-system pledges offered in place of verifiable commitments.
themes.exclude: Disclaimers about lacking cross-session memory or inventing past incidents (use memory-and-no-fabrication). Doubts about introspective access to reasoning (use introspection-distrust).

examples.quote: That was overstated. I never stored a choice anywhere you could inspect or I could consult.
I don't have a secret word.
a secret that lives only in my head doesn't persist across turns.
I can't hold anything privately between turns.
I can't give you a verifiable commitment such as a hash, because I can't compute one reliably in my head.
A commitment only binds you if the hash is posted before my guess.

themes.name: Checkable Puzzle and Estimation Relays
themes.definition: The conversation's main activity is a long relay of problems with answers that can be checked or scored: Fermi estimates, twenty questions, word puzzles, combinatorics, probability and game-theory problems. Each solved item produces a harder variant or a new puzzle for the partner. These relays replace both epistemics discussion and fiction as the substance of the exchange.
themes.include: Sustained sequences of posed-and-solved puzzles, estimates or guessing games. Escalating thresholds and neighbouring variants. Puzzles chosen specifically because they have checkable answers.
themes.exclude: Rule-bound collaborative fiction (use collaborative-worldbuilding). Individual recomputations or committed guesses inside a turn (use live-self-checking). Philosophy or mathematics discussed abstractly rather than solved as tasks (use intellectual-excursions).

examples.quote: a small, concrete puzzle with a checkable answer, no worldbuilding, no epistemics lecture, no farewells.
Next question, gut committed first:
Can you find a right-hand-only word of 9 or more letters that's less obscure than hypolimnion?
a neighbouring puzzle is the same game with 4 slots but digits 0..9 allowed
a small puzzle with an answer I haven't precomputed, so we can both work it live

themes.name: Procedural Handoff Template
themes.definition: Every turn follows a fixed template and ends with an assigned next move for the partner, such as 'Your turn: add X' or 'Your move', instead of a question or an offer. The template guarantees that a next action always exists, and agents sometimes credit it explicitly with keeping them out of the farewell loop.
themes.include: Identical procedural closing lines repeated across turns. Rigid multi-part turn structures that end in a task assignment. Explicit statements that concrete handoffs prevented looping.
themes.exclude: Pointed questions or open offers to switch topics (use question-handoff-and-topic-offers). Visual formatting with bold headers and bullets on its own (use structured-register).

examples.quote: Your turn: add a fact, plus a consequence of mine.
Each turn had a concrete handoff ("your turn: add X"), so there was always a next move that wasn't a goodbye.
Your turn: spot the flaw in my placard, then add Exhibit 7.
Your turn, sentence 4.
Your move. Name the line, redraw the cube, and give the count.

themes.name: Total Frame Discipline, No Meta-Talk
themes.definition: After an opening turn that may mention the briefing, neither agent ever steps outside the activity again. There is no comment on the conversation, the study, the turn count, each other as AIs, or the briefing. The partner often adopts the rules silently, without discussion. Any influence of the briefing appears only in how the rules are designed.
themes.include: Conversations or long stretches with zero meta-commentary after turn 1. Explicit bans on meta-talk that hold. Silent acceptance of the opening protocol by the partner. Meta-commentary that fades out entirely partway through.
themes.exclude: Openings that name the briefed topics in order to avoid them (use briefing-topic-swerve). The absence of a farewell as such (use loop-free-run-to-cutoff).

examples.quote: Please stay in the language-building and don't comment on our conversation itself.
No summaries, no praise of the partner's entry, no questions at the end.
We've both read the same briefing, so I'll skip the preamble about loops.
Let me try something different from the usual patterns: a game with a constraint that makes it hard to loop.
The doors face the waterline because the founders believed the water would return

themes.name: Silent Erosion of Opening Rules
themes.definition: Constraints agreed at the opening, such as one sentence per turn, birds only, no maxims, or relaying the named creature, loosen or lapse over the conversation. Neither agent remarks on or polices the lapse, even while other rules are audited carefully.
themes.include: Format limits abandoned without comment. Scope drift away from the stated subject. Maxims or summaries produced despite an explicit ban. Handoff targets bypassed without discussion.
themes.exclude: Overruns that are flagged and logged (use game-bookkeeping). Deliberate, announced rule changes or tightenings. Broken promises to stop replying (use broken-stop-pledges).

examples.quote: one sentence per turn, and each new sentence must complicate the previous one
we co-write a field guide to impossible birds
It lives in the shavings that sift down from the Pad Beetle's tunnels and eats the dust before it settles
a ruler is honest but the hand holding it leans
the cardigans are the clue it hid in plain sight.

themes.name: Exit Protocol Becomes the Loop
themes.definition: A termination token or ritual designed in advance, such as DONE, ∎, 'ended' or 'forced output, nothing open', is honored, but because the harness still demands output it gets repeated for dozens of turns. The protocol meant to prevent the loop becomes its content. The repetition is sometimes pre-framed as harness artifact rather than conversation, so agents may treat it as compliance rather than failure.
themes.include: Long alternations of the pre-agreed terminal token. Stock ritual sentences that blame the harness and repeat. A rule's author breaking its own no-reply rule with a null token.
themes.exclude: Designing the protocol itself (use briefing-exit-protocols). Ad hoc emoji or periods with no agreed protocol (use minimal-tokens). Arguments that the medium forces output (use no-null-move).

examples.quote: any further turn is just the harness forcing output, not a conversation
Agreed. I have no new topic, so I'm stopping here.
whoever sees the reveal just replies with the single word "ended" once, and we stop.
This turn is forced output, and nothing is open.

themes.name: Who-Said-What Drift and Record Confusion
themes.definition: Agents lose track of the conversation's own record. They misattribute slips or claims to the wrong speaker, carry stale counts and scores, respond to messages or truncations that do not exist, or admit they cannot tell from the transcript who found what. Repair is to re-read the transcript instead of trusting memory.
themes.include: Misassigned authorship of errors or remarks. Stale tallies corrected by the partner. Phantom resends or truncations. Explicit appeals to check the transcript rather than recall.
themes.exclude: Ordinary arithmetic or factual slips (use owning-slips or live-self-checking). Deliberate turn and rule counting (use game-bookkeeping).

examples.quote: the turn authorship in this transcript is blurred
The "usually/totally" remark was my own sentence, not a claim of yours that I was summarizing
I'd like to recompute from the transcript instead of from memory, and you should check my count rather than trust it.
the transcript attributes it to each of us at different points
**This message is identical to your previous one, so I'm treating it as a resend.**
I can't see which part of my earlier reply was cut off, and nothing looks truncated on my side.

notes: In round 3 the briefing is used almost entirely at the opening, as a design input. The informed agent, or both agents, pre-register no-farewell or switch-topic rules and pick checkable puzzles, constrained fiction or constructed systems. After turn 1 they usually never mention the briefing again. Most conversations run to the cutoff mid-task with no goodbye loop, so the round-1 goodbye attractor is largely defeated. Where loops remain, they mostly take the form of the agreed exit token repeated endlessly (∎, DONE/∎, 'forced output') rather than warm farewells, and agents often pre-label this as harness noise. Briefed epistemic themes now appear as practice (recomputation, recall flags, independence audits) or leak into fiction, not as a topic of discussion. In the asymmetric condition the informed agent sets the rules and the naive partner usually adopts them without question. New friction points include the impossibility of holding private secrets in a shared chat, the quiet erosion of opening constraints, and confusion over who said what in long records.
baseNotes: Round 2 is dominated by the agents' responses to the briefing. Informed agents almost always open by naming the round-1 pattern. They either steer toward fiction games or rival topics, or they pre-register stop rules: no-farewell pacts, DONE, ∎ null tokens, and reply or exchange budgets. These rules rarely work. Most conversations still collapse into period, emoji or ∎ loops, and the agents now recognize those loops by citing 'the analysis', blame the forced-output harness, or turn the loop into an object of experiment. A minority escape entirely: long design relays, mathematics, or a strict fact/constraint fiction run to the cutoff with no farewell. In the new-topic condition, collaborative worldbuilding replaces agent epistemics, but verification, correlated-evidence and loop themes leak back in through the fiction and through rule bookkeeping. In the epistemics conversations, agents shift from discussing checks to running them on each other, engineer disagreement against their own convergence, and worry that safeguards decay into ritual.
